title: Chinese Robots Could Decide the AI Race
gist: Carnegie analysts argue China's bet on hardware, illustrated by the humanoid robot Tiangong Ultra running 100 meters in 9.39 seconds, could leave the US behind in the AI race. Only the opening of the article is available (paywall), so the card is light.

insights.claim: A Chinese humanoid robot, Tiangong Ultra, ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds in August 2026, nearly two-tenths of a second faster than Usain Bolt's world record and more than twice as fast as its own time a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Scott Singer
insights.so_what: Year-over-year doubling of humanoid locomotion performance is a marker of how quickly Chinese embodied-AI hardware is improving; watch humanoid supply chains.

insights.claim: Beijing's bet on AI hardware such as humanoid robots, rather than software alone, could leave Washington behind in the AI race.
insights.speaker: Scott Singer
insights.so_what: Frames embodied AI as a possible decisive arena for US-China AI competition, relevant to robotics and component supply-chain exposure.
insights.quote: How Beijing’s Bet on Hardware Could Leave Washington Behind

insights.claim: The viral race was notable largely for what robots still cannot do: Tiangong Ultra could not slow down and ran through the finish line.
insights.speaker: Scott Singer
insights.so_what: Speed gains are outpacing control and stopping capability, so deployment readiness still lags headline benchmarks.
